body:
Why Civilian Protection Is Central to Security

The purpose of internal security is not simply to stop unlawful activity. It is also to protect people so that they can live, work, travel and exercise their rights without serious threats of violence. After a major incident, the safety of victims, medical assistance, preservation of public order and reliable communication are immediate public responsibilities.

Security measures can affect personal liberty, movement and access to public places. In a constitutional democracy, such measures must have a lawful basis and remain subject to appropriate safeguards and oversight.

Fundamental Rights and Public Safety

ProvisionBasic protectionSecurity-related significance
Article 14Equality before the law and equal protection of the lawsPublic authorities must not act arbitrarily or discriminate unlawfully.
Article 19Specified freedoms of citizens, including speech and peaceful assemblyRestrictions must satisfy the applicable constitutional grounds and requirements.
Article 21Protection of life and personal libertyDeprivation of liberty must follow a legally valid, fair, just and reasonable procedure.

These rights do not prevent lawful investigation or proportionate public-safety regulation. They require the state to exercise its powers within legal limits. Article 19 freedoms are not absolute: the Constitution permits specified reasonable restrictions, including on relevant grounds such as the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the state and public order, depending on the particular freedom involved.

Evidence, Fair Trial and Accountability

A person accused of an offence must not be treated as already convicted. In a criminal trial, the prosecution must establish guilt according to the applicable legal standard, ordinarily beyond reasonable doubt. The accused must have a meaningful opportunity to defend themselves, and the court must decide the matter impartially on the evidence.

This distinction is especially important when incidents attract intense public attention. An accusation, arrest, official statement, investigation report and final judicial finding are not equivalent forms of proof.

Security and legality are not opposites. A legitimate security response protects civilians, investigates offences under law and preserves the safeguards that make public institutions accountable.

Domestic Law Enforcement and Armed Conflict Are Different Contexts

When authorities respond to an ordinary criminal incident, domestic criminal law, constitutional guarantees and applicable human-rights obligations are central. When a situation legally qualifies as an armed conflict, international humanitarian law also regulates conduct during hostilities. Not every terrorism investigation or security alert constitutes an armed conflict.

Three important humanitarian-law principles in armed conflict are:

  • Distinction: parties must distinguish civilians and civilian objects from lawful military objectives. Deliberate attacks against civilians are prohibited.
  • Proportionality: an attack is prohibited when the expected incidental civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated.
  • Precautions: parties must take feasible measures to avoid or minimize civilian harm.

These are legal safeguards governing armed conflict; they are not permission to treat ordinary domestic policing as warfare. Nor does invoking national security automatically remove constitutional protections.

What Citizens Can Do During a Security Emergency

For an immediate emergency in India, citizens can use 112, the nationwide emergency number under the Emergency Response Support System (ERSS). The system supports coordination with police, medical, fire and other emergency services.

Citizens should prioritize their own safety, follow directions issued by authorized emergency personnel, provide accurate information when reporting an incident and avoid obstructing rescue activities. They should also avoid circulating unverified images, casualty figures, communal allegations or identifying details of victims. Such restraint reduces confusion and helps protect both safety and dignity.

Prelims focus

  • Article 14: equality before the law and equal protection of the laws.
  • Article 19: specified citizen freedoms, subject to constitutionally permitted restrictions.
  • Article 21: protection of life and personal liberty.
  • 112: nationwide emergency number under ERSS.
  • International humanitarian law: distinction, proportionality and precautions protect civilians during armed conflict.
  • Trap: Security allegations do not remove the requirement of lawful procedure or establish guilt.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 11, Indian Constitution at Work, Chapter 2, 'Rights in the Indian Constitution', printed pp. 27–35; NCERT, Class 8, Social and Political Life III, Chapter 6, 'Understanding Our Criminal Justice System', printed pp. 72–75; Ministry of Home Affairs, 'Emergency Response Support System (ERSS)', official scheme description, consulted 16 November 2026; International Committee of the Red Cross, 'FAQ: Rules of War' and 'Frequently Asked Questions: International Armed Conflict', sections on distinction, proportionality and precautions, consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Emergency protection involves assistance to civilians as well as maintaining public order.

pictures.caption: A responsible security response combines protection, lawful action and accountability.

title: Civilian Protection, Constitutional Rights and Responsible State Response

body:
Why Gujarat Has a Distinct Security Context

Gujarat's geography makes both land-border and maritime-security issues relevant. The state borders Pakistan in the Kachchh region and has an extensive coastline along the Arabian Sea. Its coast supports fishing communities, commercial ports, shipping, industrial activity and offshore facilities.

These activities are important for livelihoods and the economy. They also create a need for lawful monitoring, emergency preparedness and cooperation among public authorities. Maritime security must protect legitimate trade and fishing while responding to threats such as unauthorized cross-border activity, smuggling and possible infiltration.

Important Geographical References

Kachchh is significant because it combines an international land-border context with coastal and creek areas. Sir Creek is associated with the India–Pakistan border region and the broader question of security in the creek area. The Gulf of Kachchh is important for maritime trade and coastal installations.

Deendayal Port, formerly known as Kandla Port, is located near the head of the Gulf of Kachchh. It is a major gateway for trade serving western and northwestern India. Its earlier name, Kandla, remains relevant when reading older geography textbooks and historical documents.

Land border and maritime security are related but not identical. Security responsibilities differ between the international land-border area, coastal communities, ports and the wider maritime domain.

Who Protects India's Maritime Areas?

India's coastal-security arrangements require coordination among the Indian Navy, Indian Coast Guard and State Marine Police, together with other relevant authorities.

InstitutionBroad responsibilityConnection with Gujarat
Indian NavyOverall maritime-security and maritime-defence responsibilitiesNational maritime coordination and defence preparedness
Indian Coast GuardMaritime law-enforcement and coastal-security responsibilities, including coordination in territorial watersProtection of maritime interests and engagement with coastal communities
State Marine PoliceCoastal policing under the state systemPublic-safety and law-enforcement responsibilities near coastal communities
Border Security Force (BSF)Border-security duties in assigned areasIts Water Wing has been specifically identified in official reporting concerning Sir Creek.

Other participants may include port authorities, Customs, fisheries departments and local administration. Their roles concern legitimate movement, regulation, information-sharing and public safety. A fishing boat, a port installation and a land-border location do not automatically fall under an identical institutional arrangement.

Coastal Security Scheme: Before and After 2008

The Ministry of Home Affairs introduced the Coastal Security Scheme to strengthen the infrastructure of coastal police organizations. Phase I operated from 2005 to 2011. This is an important chronological fact: the scheme began before the terrorist attacks in Mumbai on 26 November 2008.

The attacks of 26/11 gave further urgency to strengthening coastal security. Subsequent improvements placed emphasis on coordination among maritime agencies and on the readiness of coastal police and other stakeholders. It would therefore be incorrect to say that India's Coastal Security Scheme began only after the Mumbai attacks.

Fishing Communities and Public Cooperation

Fishing communities have an important relationship with the sea and coastal administration. Their safety depends on accurate weather and public advisories, access to assistance and communication with authorized authorities. Government programmes have included interaction with fishermen to improve coastal-security awareness.

Residents and fishing communities can support public safety by reporting credible concerns to authorized authorities rather than confronting suspected persons or spreading unverified allegations. Legitimate fishing activity and cross-border criminal activity must not be confused merely because both involve movement at sea.

Current Affairs: Sea Vigil-26

The Ministry of Defence announced on 11 November 2026 that the 5th edition of Sea Vigil, named Sea Vigil-26, was being held from 11 to 19 November 2026, with the Indian Navy as the lead coordinating agency. The announced schedule included a Coastal Defence and Security Readiness Evaluation phase from 11 to 17 November, followed by a sea phase on 18 and 19 November.

Sea Vigil was conceptualized in 2018 to assess measures introduced to strengthen maritime security following the 2008 Mumbai attacks. Sea Vigil-26 involves coastal states and Union Territories, maritime agencies and coastal communities.

Status at the content cutoff of 16 November 2026: the announced exercise period was still underway. Its eventual findings, completion and outcomes should not be presented as established facts on that date.

Prelims focus

  • Sir Creek: relevant to Gujarat's India–Pakistan border and creek-security context.
  • Deendayal Port: formerly Kandla Port, near the Gulf of Kachchh.
  • Coastal Security Scheme Phase I: 2005–2011.
  • 26/11: Mumbai terrorist attacks on 26 November 2008, followed by further coastal-security strengthening.
  • Sea Vigil-26: 5th edition; Indian Navy lead coordinator; announced dates 11–19 November 2026.
  • Trap: The Coastal Security Scheme was not first introduced after 26/11.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, India: People and Economy, Chapter 11, 'International Trade', printed pp. 129–131, for Kandla's geographical and trade significance; Ministry of Home Affairs, 'Coastal Security Scheme', Phase I and Phase II descriptions, consulted 16 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Infiltration along Gujarat Coast', 7 March 2018, Release 1522938; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Indian Navy to Coordinate Fifth Edition of Pan-India Coastal Defence Exercise Sea Vigil-26', 11 November 2026, Release 2335093, consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Coastal security depends on cooperation among agencies with different responsibilities.

pictures.caption: Fishing communities are part of Gujarat's coastal economy and public-safety environment.

title: Gujarat's Border, Coast and Maritime-Security Significance

body:
Why a Significant Security Event Must Be Analysed Carefully

A major security event should be studied by separating the triggering incident, the government's stated objectives, the measures announced, the reported consequences and the applicable safeguards. These are different kinds of information. A government's statement about why it acted should be accurately attributed to that government; it should not automatically be converted into an independently established finding.

Operation Sindoor, announced by India in May 2025, provides an example of how a terrorist incident can develop into a wider cross-border security crisis. The account below distinguishes dated official announcements from broader legal and analytical conclusions.

The Triggering Incident: Pahalgam, 22 April 2025

A terrorist attack at Pahalgam on 22 April 2025 killed 26 civilians. India's Ministry of Defence subsequently described the victims as 25 Indian nationals and 1 Nepali national.

The attack illustrates the human-security dimension of terrorism: civilians were the immediate victims, while fear and concern about safety extended more widely. It also became the stated trigger for subsequent Indian government action involving cross-border security.

India's Announcement of Operation Sindoor: 7 May 2025

In an official announcement dated 7 May 2025, India's Ministry of Defence stated that the Indian Armed Forces had launched Operation Sindoor. The statement described the operation as targeting terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir and said that 9 sites had been targeted.

The Indian government presented the initial action as a response intended to hold those responsible for the Pahalgam attack accountable and to address infrastructure that it associated with attacks against India. It described the action as focused, measured and intended to avoid escalation.

The 7 May 2025 announcement stated that Pakistani military facilities had not been targeted in that initial action. This description must remain attached to the initial announcement. It must not be extended to all later military activity during the crisis.

Subsequent Developments and the Understanding of 10 May 2025

Further military exchanges and allegations concerning attacks and violations followed the initial announcement. Official Indian accounts described subsequent responses and expressed concerns about further escalation. These accounts should be recognized as official statements rather than treated as an independently settled record of every disputed claim.

According to India's subsequent official account, the Directors General of Military Operations of India and Pakistan reached an understanding to stop firing and military action on land, in the air and at sea with effect from 17:00 Indian Standard Time on 10 May 2025.

Such an understanding is an important de-escalation measure: it seeks to reduce immediate hostilities and the risk of further harm. It does not, by itself, establish that all disputed claims have been resolved, that every alleged violation has been independently verified, or that the underlying terrorism problem has disappeared.

Understanding Objectives, Outcomes and Consequences

QuestionWhat the record establishesNecessary qualification
What triggered the response?Pahalgam attack on 22 April 2025, killing 26 civiliansThe attack and subsequent military measures are distinct events.
What was announced?India announced Operation Sindoor on 7 May 2025 and reported targeting 9 sites.The description of the sites and objectives comes from India's official announcement.
What was the stated objective?Respond to the attack and address infrastructure India associated with terrorism.A stated objective is not identical to a verified result.
What de-escalation measure followed?An understanding to stop military action from 17:00 IST on 10 May 2025An announced halt is not necessarily a permanent political settlement.

What Safeguards Apply to a State Response?

Protection of civilians remains a central consideration in security decision-making. Responsible public policy also requires careful verification of information, appropriate public warnings, access to emergency assistance and efforts to avoid unnecessary escalation.

At the international level, the United Nations Charter provides the broader legal framework. Article 2(4) generally prohibits the threat or use of force against another state's territorial integrity or political independence. Article 51 recognizes the inherent right of individual or collective self-defence if an armed attack occurs against a UN member, until the Security Council has taken measures necessary to maintain international peace and security; measures taken in self-defence must be immediately reported to the Security Council. Whether a particular use of force satisfies international law depends on its facts and the relevant legal standards; announcing a security objective does not settle that question.

Where international humanitarian law applies because an armed conflict exists, parties must respect requirements such as distinction, proportionality and feasible precautions to protect civilians. These safeguards concern the lawfulness of conduct; they should not be confused with the political claim that an action was necessary or successful.

Lessons for Current-Affairs Understanding

The event demonstrates the connection between terrorism, civilian harm, cross-border security, national decision-making and international relations. It also shows why dated, attributed facts are essential. A learner should distinguish what occurred, what an authority said occurred, what objectives were announced, and what independent conclusions can properly be drawn.

Prelims focus

  • 22 April 2025: Pahalgam terrorist attack; 26 civilian deaths reported by India's Ministry of Defence.
  • 7 May 2025: India announced Operation Sindoor.
  • 9: number of sites described as targeted in India's initial announcement.
  • 10 May 2025, 17:00 IST: effective time stated for the understanding to halt military action.
  • UN Charter Article 2(4): general prohibition on the threat or use of force against states.
  • UN Charter Article 51: right of self-defence in the event of an armed attack, subject to Charter conditions.
  • Trap: The description of the initial 7 May action must not be generalized to later exchanges.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, 'Operation Sindoor: Indian Armed Forces Carried Out Precision Strike at Terrorist Camps', 7 May 2025, Release 2127370; Press Information Bureau, 'Operation SINDOOR: India's Strategic Clarity and Calculated Force', May 2025, account of the understanding effective 10 May 2025; United Nations, Charter of the United Nations, Articles 2(4) and 51, consulted 16 November 2026; International Committee of the Red Cross, 'FAQ: Rules of War', sections on distinction, proportionality and precautions, consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The sequence distinguishes the triggering attack, initial announcement and later de-escalation understanding.

title: Operation Sindoor in May 2025: Objectives, Consequences and Safeguards
